quote: Without the mark, a Spanish reader says BO-go-ta. The mark is part of the spelling, and the checker reads it like a Bogotano would.
problem: False stress in the stress lesson itself. By the rule three paragraphs up, a word ending in a vowel stresses the second-to-last syllable, so unaccented Bogota reads bo-GO-ta, never BO-go-ta. A learner who is trying to absorb the rule is told the opposite of what it predicts.
authority: Ortografia de la lengua espanola (RAE 2010), general accent rules; internal contradiction with the rule field of this script
replacement: Without the mark, a Spanish reader says bo-GO-ta, stress on the second-to-last syllable. The mark is part of the spelling, and the checker reads it like a Bogotano would.

quote:
A describing word matches the person or thing it describes: a man or a woman, one or more.

Words ending in *o* switch to *a* for a woman: *cansado*, *cansada*; *colombiano*, *colombiana*.
problem: First contact with agreement is framed entirely as sex (man or woman). Every example, Read and Pick, Your Turn and pitfall in the script is about people: 0 of the 28 examples and practice items agree with an inanimate noun. An English speaker leaves with "the a is for women", which undoes the gender lesson ("It's a label, not a meaning") and gives no model for la casa es pequena or el pan esta listo, la leche esta lista.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009), concordancia nominal; reasoning from the script g:gender-articles
replacement:
A describing word matches the noun it describes: masculine or feminine, one or more. With people that usually follows man or woman. With things it follows *el* or *la*: *el pan está listo*, *la leche está lista*.

Words ending in *o* switch to *a* for anything feminine: *cansado*, *cansada*; *colombiano*, *colombiana*.

quote: Here you only need *me* and *te*; *le*, *nos* and *les* come later.
problem: Me gusta plus a named person commonly means attraction, and in Colombia it is read that way by default. The script drills it with no warning (readAndPick[0] Me gusta Tomas, [1] Te gusta Mariana), and the fix for liking someone as a person, me cae bien, arrives at u15 without mentioning the trap either. An English speaker will say Me gusta tu hermana to a friend and mean something innocent.
authority: Usage evidence; Butt and Benjamin on gustar with persons
replacement: Here you only need *me* and *te*; *le*, *nos* and *les* come later. One warning: about a person, *me gusta* usually means you're attracted to them. For things, places and activities it's always safe.

quote: Two surprises this week: *el día* is masculine.
problem: The rule says -a is usually feminine and lists one exception. The large family in -ma (el problema, el idioma, el tema, el sistema, el programa, el clima) is never explained anywhere in the 916 scripts; a scan finds only the passing "a masculine noun like problema" in g:indefinites. La problema is the signature English-speaker error, and the node es for this very lesson contains la mano, which the script also never mentions.
authority: Nueva gramatica, genero de los sustantivos; corpus scan of all script rule, smallPrint and pitfall fields
replacement: Three surprises this week: *el día* is masculine, and so are many words in *-ma*, like *el problema* and *el idioma* (language). *La mano* (hand) is feminine despite its *-o*.

quote:
A stretch of time or an old habit takes the describing past: *Cuando era niño, vivía en Toronto.*
One moment takes the event past: *Cuando llegué a Bogotá...*
problem: Teaches the classic false equation long = imperfect, short = preterite. Length does not choose the past; viewpoint does. A learner who absorbs this writes *Hernando era taxista durante cuarenta años* or *Vivía en Toronto diez años*. It also undoes x:pret-imp (u12), which already says llovió toda la noche wraps a whole night up as one finished thing. The app's own content contradicts it: 28 A2 bank sentences, counted by hand from a regex pull, put a stated duration in the preterite (u21-0386 Hernando fue taxista durante cuarenta años; u15-0717 Hernando estuvo casado treinta años; u25-0292 Mi hijo lloró toda la noche), plus p:horas-y-horas (Rosa trabajó años y años en el café) and ch079.
authority: Nueva gramática de la lengua española (2009), chapter on tense and aspect: perfective against imperfective viewpoint, not duration; Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, preterite and imperfect chapters: the preterite is required for a completed period however long; project evidence as listed
replacement:
Spanish doesn't choose by how long something lasted. It chooses by how you look at it.
The background you're standing inside, or an old habit, takes the describing past: *Cuando era niño, vivía en Toronto.*
An event that moves the story on takes the event past: *Cuando llegué a Bogotá...*
A long stretch can still be an event if you wrap it up as one finished thing: *Hernando fue taxista cuarenta años.*

quote: Being a kid is a whole stretch of time, so the describing past: *era*.
problem: Same length fallacy in the answer feedback, the place a learner reads it right after a success.
authority: Nueva gramática de la lengua española (2009), tense and aspect chapter; Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish
replacement: You're setting the background and looking at it from inside, so the describing past: *era*.

quote: Almost. Childhood isn't one moment, it's a whole stretch, so *era*.
problem: The correction is right, the reason is false: long stretches take the preterite whenever they are presented as finished (u19-0294 Hernando trabajó de taxista durante cuarenta años).
authority: Nueva gramática de la lengua española (2009), tense and aspect chapter; Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish
replacement: Almost. *Cuando era niño* sets the background for what comes next, so *era*. It isn't about length: *Viví diez años en Toronto* is fine, because that wraps the ten years up as one finished thing.

quote: Mariana dijo que va a llamar.
problem: Labels correct, everyday Spanish as a mistake. When what was said still holds or is still to come, the present stays: Mariana dijo que va a llamar means the call is still expected. English allows the same (Mariana said she's going to call), so the why, the same shift English makes, is also wrong. The bank itself has u26-0033 Vale me dijo que se va para Medellín. The pitfall shows on a card and in Reference, and yourTurn[5] has no accept for this form, so a correct answer is marked wrong.
authority: Nueva gramática de la lengua española (2009), sequence of tenses (consecutio temporum) and the double-access reading; Bosque and Demonte, Gramática descriptiva, chapter on tense in subordinate clauses; usage in u26-0033
replacement: {"wrong": "Mariana dijo que iba llamar.", "right": "Mariana dijo que iba a llamar.", "why": "Almost. Don't drop the little *a*: *iba a llamar*, just like *voy a llamar*."}

quote: Quick test: if English could add in general, Spanish wants the article.
problem: The take-away test fails on the lesson's own hook. I don't drink coffee in general at night, and I drink coffee, in general, every day, both pass the test, yet the script requires No tomo café and marks Tomo el café todos los días as wrong in pitfalls[3]. The real split is the whole category against some of it, not generality. A learner who trusts the test writes Tomo el café and Compro el pan for habits.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, definite article chapter: generic nouns take the article, but a noun that is the object of verbs like tomar, comprar, tener denotes an unspecified amount and stays bare; Nueva gramática de la lengua española (2009), bare nouns chapter
replacement: Quick test: do you mean all of it, the whole category, as when you say what it's like or how you feel about it? Spanish wants the article: *Me gusta el café.* Do you mean some of it, as when you buy, drink or have it? No article: *Tomo café.*

quote: No dudo que tengas razón.
problem: Correct, common Spanish is struck through as a mistake. Textbooks teach the indicative here, and that is a fair default, but negated dudar admits both moods: the indicative asserts, the subjunctive concedes. The course itself uses the subjunctive here: all 9 bank rows with *no dudo que* (u44-0915 to u44-1533) are subjunctive, and none is indicative, so the learner is told a form is wrong and later drilled on nothing else. Tested through the real card code: typing it fails with the hint "Check the verb ending: when does it happen?"
authority: Decisive: internal contradiction with app/content/bank/u44.json. Also Nueva gramatica ch. 25 and Butt and Benjamin ch. 16, from memory, not checkable online; native speaker reports on tomisimo and Lawless Spanish

quote: The flip side: *No dudo que* means you are sure, so the plain verb comes back: *No dudo que tienes razón*.
problem: Presents the indicative as the only option. A good rule keeps the plain verb as the default and says the other exists, which also follows from the course's own model: stating it as a fact versus granting it.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25); Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, subjunctive chapter (16)
replacement: The flip side: *No dudo que* says you are sure, so the plain verb is the natural choice: *No dudo que tienes razón*. You will also meet the wish form here, often before a *pero*: *No dudo que tengas razón, pero...* Both are correct.

quote: *No dudo que* means you are sure, so the plain verb comes back: *tienes*.
problem: The fill-in offers *tienes* or *tengas* with accept empty, so the correct *tengas* is marked wrong. Either accept both or remove the item.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25)
replacement: Set accept to ["No dudo que tengas razón."] and why to: *No dudo que* means you are sure, so the plain verb is the natural choice: *tienes*.

quote: Llámame antes que salgas.
problem: Correct Spanish is struck through. *Antes que* and *antes de que* are both valid before a clause. The real slip English speakers make is dropping *que*.
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry antes (equal examples: Llegara antes que anochezca, Llegara antes de que anochezca), read via search snippet of rae.es/dpd/antes
replacement: {"wrong":"Llámame antes de salgas.","right":"Llámame antes de que salgas.","why":"Almost. When a new person does the second action, you need *que*: *antes de que*."}

quote: Dijo que vendrá.
problem: *Dijo que vendrá* is correct whenever the coming is still ahead of the speaker now, and it is very common in Latin America. The rule that the future must shift is false as an absolute. The form is only wrong when the event lies in the past story.
authority: Nueva gramatica, ch. 24, double access, from memory; standard accounts agree the form needs the present perspective
replacement: {"wrong":"Ayer Vale dijo que vendrá, pero no vino.","right":"Ayer Vale dijo que vendría, pero no vino.","why":"Almost. She did not come, so the coming belongs to the past story: use the would form. *Dijo que vendrá* only works if it is still ahead of you now."}

quote: Almost. A rate such as "three times a day" is always *por*.
problem: False. *Tres veces al día* and *una vez a la semana* are at least as common, and the bank itself has 45 such rows against 10 with *por* (u03-0538, u09-0013, u35-0090). A learner who trusts "always" will think the commonest form is wrong.
authority: Usage; internal contradiction with app/content/bank/u03.json and u09.json
replacement: Almost. A rate never takes *para*. Say *por día* or, just as often, *al día*: *tres veces al día*.

quote: Never add *pero* next to any of them. Each one already carries the "but".
problem: *Pero aun así* is normal Spanish. The bank has 9 rows, all in u38 and u39, the units that teach this (u38-0316, u38-0317, u38-0354, u39-0041, u39-0047, u39-0786), and this script's own PERSONAL prompt says *Estoy cansado, pero aun así…*. Only *pero sin embargo* is frowned on.
authority: Usage; internal contradiction within app/content/scripts/g_concession-despite.json
replacement: Don't add *pero* in front of *sin embargo*: it already carries the "but". *Pero aun así* is fine: *Estoy cansado, pero aun así voy.*

quote: Spanish marks that by switching the verb to the wish form: *tengas*, *esté*, *sea*, *venga*.
problem: The label "wish form" gives the wrong reason for the mood. Nobody wishes anything in *No creo que tengas razón*, *Dudo que venga*, *Es una pena que cierren* or *No conozco a nadie que sepa*. In *Me da miedo que venga* the event is the opposite of a wish. A learner who uses the label as a cue will choose the indicative after doubt, fear and dislike. The learner-visible label also fragments: across the 224 B1 scripts the same form is called wish form, wish ending, changed ending, asking form, other vowel, opposite ending, request ending, new verb form and -e style verb. Replace by one name and one concept everywhere (see report section 6).
authority: Nueva gramatica, chapter on mood (25): the indicative asserts, the subjunctive does not; pedagogical judgement

quote: If you mean people in general, skip *que* and use the plain verb: *Es normal tener miedo.* *Es mejor llamar antes.*
problem: Three days earlier (u28 d1) "plain verb" was defined as the indicative: *tienes*, *está*, *es*. Here it means the infinitive. Following the earlier definition gives *Es normal tiene miedo*. Of 23 B1 scripts that say plain verb or plain form, some mean indicative and some infinitive.
authority: Internal: g:subj-opinion-negated smallPrint "The plain form is the indicative."
replacement: If you mean people in general, skip *que* and use the infinitive: *Es normal tener miedo.* *Es mejor llamar antes.*

quote: Later this week you'll add *me da pena que*, *me da rabia que* and *me da miedo que*. Same shape.
problem: The node title and example promise *siento que*, but the script never uses it and no script teaches the meaning switch. *Siento que estés triste* is I'm sorry you're sad; *Siento que estás triste* is I sense you're sad. Both moods are in the bank (u30-0037, u30-1135, u25-0392), and p:sentir-lo-de strikes the indicative through as wrong. This is the sharpest mood contrast in the emotion family and English speakers will not guess it.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25); Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, subjunctive chapter (16)
replacement: Later this week you'll add *me da pena que*, *me da rabia que* and *me da miedo que*. Same shape. One trap: *siento que* with the wish form means I'm sorry: *Siento que estés triste.* With the plain verb it means I feel or I sense: *Siento que estás triste.*

quote: *Igual* at the start also means *maybe*, in casual talk.
problem: Wrong dialect, presented as Bogotá speech. The DPD marks *igual* for *maybe* as colloquial Spain. In American Spanish a sentence-initial *igual* is documented as concessive, *anyway*, *regardless*: *Igual voy* is I'm going anyway. So the 21 bank rows likely mean something else in the setting they are written for: *Igual hace frío en la noche, lleva chaqueta* would read as It's cold at night anyway, not It might be cold. *De pronto* for maybe is correct Colombian usage and should stay. The rest of the rule, the examples, pitfalls[1] and the bank rows need rewriting with it.
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry igual: used in the colloquial language of Spain with indicative for a lo mejor, posiblemente (via search snippet of rae.es/dpd/igual). American concessive igual: Garcia Negroni and Marcovecchio 2013, Llopis Cardona. No source found specific to Colombia, so a Colombian speaker should confirm the replacement wording
replacement: *Igual* at the start of a sentence usually means something else in Latin America: *anyway*. *Igual voy* is I'm going anyway. In Spain it can mean maybe, so don't be surprised if a Spanish friend uses it that way.

quote: Listen to people in Bogotá for an afternoon and you will hear *de pronto* and *igual* all the time, and neither means what the dictionary says. In everyday speech, both mean *maybe*.
problem: Same issue.
authority: As above
replacement: Listen to people in Bogotá for an afternoon and you will hear *de pronto* and *igual* all the time. *De pronto* means *maybe*. *Igual* usually means *anyway*.

quote: Mi hermano y mi prima llegaron tarde; este trajo pan y aquella trajo jugo.
problem: The lesson on this exact point contains a reversed sentence. *Este* is the nearer item and must agree with *mi prima*, so it should be *esta*; *aquel* points to the earlier *mi hermano*. As written, gender forces *este* onto the brother and *aquella* onto the cousin, which reverses the rule and contradicts the English ("the latter brought bread").
authority: g:referring-back rule; Nueva gramatica on demonstratives
replacement: Mi hermano y mi prima llegaron tarde; esta trajo pan y aquel trajo jugo.

quote: Simón y Vale están en la sala. Este habla y esta escucha.
problem: The lesson on this exact point contains a reversed sentence. *Este* can only be Simón, the first named, so *este* is pointing at the former, and the English says "the latter talks". Two proximal demonstratives in a row also defeat the contrast. To match the English: Vale (latter) talks, Simón (former) listens.
authority: g:referring-back rule
replacement: Simón y Vale están en la sala. Esta habla y aquel escucha.

quote: Vale tiene una hermana y un hermano. Esta vive en Cali y aquel vive en Bogotá.
problem: The lesson on this exact point contains a reversed sentence. The last named is *un hermano*, so the latter must be *este*. *Esta* can only be the sister, the first named. Spanish and English disagree on who lives where.
authority: g:referring-back rule
replacement: Vale tiene una hermana y un hermano. Este vive en Cali y aquella vive en Bogotá.

quote: Igual vendo el carro.
problem: 21 rows train *igual* as maybe, with English "might". In Colombia these read as *anyway*: *Igual vendo el carro* is I'm selling the car anyway. See claim on p:de-pronto-igual rule. Each row needs retranslating as anyway, or rewriting with *de pronto*.
authority: As p:de-pronto-igual claim

quote:
*-ar* verbs take *-e*: *llueva*, *pague*, *insista*.
*-er* and *-ir* verbs take *-a*: *tenga*, *haga*, *ofrezca* (it is *-ca* here).
problem: Two of the three verbs filed under -ar are not -ar verbs, and their forms end in -a, not -e. Llueva is from llover, insista from insistir. Only pague fits. A learner who trusts the rule cannot derive the subjunctive of any verb, and it undoes the vowel flip taught in B1.
authority: Basic Spanish verb morphology: llover is -er, insistir is -ir, pagar is -ar. The script contradicts itself: yourTurn[0].why says llueva has the -a ending of llover, yourTurn[4].why says insistir is an -ir verb that takes -a.
replacement:
*-ar* verbs take *-e*: *pague*, *firme*, *cierre*.
*-er* and *-ir* verbs take *-a*: *llueva*, *insista*, *tenga*, *haga*, *ofrezca*.

quote: They always take the subjunctive.
problem: False for siempre que, one of the four connectors listed. As whenever it takes the indicative, and the course itself teaches that at u17 in g:cuando-indicative (Siempre que llueve, vendemos más tinto), with more in the bank at u46-1303. The learner is told a rule that contradicts a lesson they already passed.
authority: g:cuando-indicative examples[3]; RAE DPD on siempre que is the place to confirm the conditional sense; bank u17-t-cuando-indicative-0028, u46-1303.
replacement: As conditions they take the subjunctive. *Siempre que* can also mean whenever, and then it keeps the ordinary verb, as you already know: *Siempre que llueve, vendemos más tinto.*

quote: *en caso de que*: in case
problem: English in case usually means a precaution taken now, whatever happens. En caso de que means if it should happen. Glossing one as the other leads learners to say Llevo paraguas en caso de que llueva where natives say por si llueve, and to misread notices. It has already produced mismatched bank cards (see the bank claims).
authority: Spanish pedagogical grammars agree: por si + indicative for precaution, en caso de que + subjunctive for a contingency (Yepes, Spanish Grammar Manual; elon.io Latin America course). Butt and Benjamin, ch. on conditional sentences, to confirm.
replacement: *en caso de que*: if, in the event that

quote: With these four phrases, use the wish form, and never *-ría*.
problem: Por si, the native way to say in case, is not taught anywhere. Measured: 0 of 916 scripts contain it, it is not in the graph as a chunk or pattern, and it occurs in 4 of 72,693 bank sentences. An English speaker needs it constantly, and it takes the indicative, which this lesson teaches them to avoid.
authority: Measured with a script across app/content/scripts, graph and bank. Grammar as above.
replacement:
With these four phrases, use the wish form, and never *-ría*.

English *in case* hides two ideas. If you act only when the thing happens, use *en caso de que*: *En caso de que llueva, la reunión es adentro.* If you act now, just to be safe, use *por si* with the ordinary verb: *Llévate un abrigo por si hace frío.* Test: would you do it anyway? Then it is *por si*.

quote:
Put *no* in front and you are no longer vouching, so the verb after *que* switches to the past form that ends in *-ra*: *estaba* becomes *estuviera*, *era* becomes *fuera*, *tenía* becomes *tuviera*, *llegó* becomes *llegara*, *sonó* becomes *sonara*.

*No vi que estuviera enojada.* *No dijo que fuera urgente.* It is the same switch as after *no creo que*.

So does *No es que no quiera, es que no puedo*: the first half is the thing you deny.

English keeps one verb for both. Spanish changes it.
problem: Negation does not force the switch here. Unlike no creo que, these verbs leave a choice, and the choice carries meaning. No vi que estabas ahí says you were there and I missed it. No vi que estuvieras ahí says I saw no sign that you were. No dijo que era urgente says it was urgent and he left that out. The rule erases the distinction and the model the learner needs, and the course already teaches the indicative after no sabía que and no me di cuenta de que.
authority: Mood after negated verbs of perception and communication depends on whether the speaker presupposes the clause: NGLE ch. 25 (modo), Bosque and Demonte 1999 ch. 49, Butt and Benjamin ch. 16 (subjunctive). I could not reach NGLE text during this audit and some learner sources state the flat rule, so the verifier should test with native judgement and CORPES. Internal evidence: u38-0541 No me di cuenta de que estabas aquí, u12-0096 No sabía que venías, ch209 Yo no le dije que hablaba bonito.
replacement:
Put *no* in front and you now have a choice, and it says who is vouching.

Keep the ordinary verb and you still vouch for it: it was true, and someone missed it or left it out. *No vi que estabas ahí.* You were there, and I missed you. *No dijo que era urgente.* It was urgent, and he left that out.

Switch to the *-ra* form and nobody vouches: *estaba* becomes *estuviera*, *era* becomes *fuera*, *tenía* becomes *tuviera*, *llegó* becomes *llegara*. *No dije que fuera urgente.* I never claimed that. *No vi que estuviera enojada.* I saw no sign of it.

With *nadie* or *nada*, use the *-ra* form: *No vi que llegara nadie.* To say you missed something happening, you can also use the plain verb: *No oí sonar el teléfono.*

*No es que* always denies, so it always takes the wish form: *No es que no quiera, es que no puedo.*

English keeps one verb for both. Spanish tells you who stands behind the claim.

quote: No vi que Vale estaba enojada.
problem: Marks correct Spanish as wrong. This is the natural sentence when she was angry and I failed to notice, as in the everyday Perdón, no vi que estabas ahí. The English of the same card, I didn't see that Vale was angry, normally presupposes she was.
authority: Mood after negated verbs of perception and communication depends on whether the speaker presupposes the clause: NGLE ch. 25 (modo), Bosque and Demonte 1999 ch. 49, Butt and Benjamin ch. 16 (subjunctive). I could not reach NGLE text during this audit and some learner sources state the flat rule, so the verifier should test with native judgement and CORPES. Internal evidence: u38-0541 No me di cuenta de que estabas aquí, u12-0096 No sabía que venías, ch209 Yo no le dije que hablaba bonito.
replacement: {"wrong": "No vi que estuvieras ahí. (you know the person was there)", "right": "No vi que estabas ahí.", "why": "You know the person was there, so you still vouch for it: *estabas*. *Estuvieras* would doubt it."}

quote: No dijo que era urgente.
problem: Marks correct Spanish as wrong. It means it was urgent and he did not mention it. A later chapter does exactly this: ch209 Yesid: Yo no le dije que hablaba bonito.
authority: Mood after negated verbs of perception and communication depends on whether the speaker presupposes the clause: NGLE ch. 25 (modo), Bosque and Demonte 1999 ch. 49, Butt and Benjamin ch. 16 (subjunctive). I could not reach NGLE text during this audit and some learner sources state the flat rule, so the verifier should test with native judgement and CORPES. Internal evidence: u38-0541 No me di cuenta de que estabas aquí, u12-0096 No sabía que venías, ch209 Yo no le dije que hablaba bonito.
replacement: {"wrong": "No dijo que era urgente. (you doubt it was urgent at all)", "right": "No dijo que fuera urgente.", "why": "*Era* would mean it was urgent and he left that out. To avoid vouching for it, use *fuera*."}

quote: No dudo que el proyecto es bueno, pero es muy caro.
problem: Marks correct, indeed the commoner, Spanish as wrong, and directly contradicts g:subj-doubt pitfalls[1], which marks the subjunctive wrong after the same words. A learner is penalised in opposite directions at B1 and B2.
authority: Two lessons contradict each other. Learner references mostly give indicative after no dudo que, while the subjunctive also occurs, especially when conceding, so neither form is wrong. I found no NGLE text on this; check NGLE ch. 25 and DPD dudar.
replacement: {"wrong": "Dudo que el proyecto sea bueno, pero es muy caro.", "right": "No dudo que el proyecto sea bueno, pero es muy caro.", "why": "Almost. *Dudo que* says you think it isn't good. To grant the point first, you need *no dudo que*."}

quote: When you retell a conversation after the fact, everything takes one step back, in time and in place. Spanish does it as faithfully as English.
problem: Everything is too strong. If the content still holds, Spanish keeps the tense (Dijo que viene mañana, when tomorrow has not come), and the preterite is often retained, especially in Latin America (Dijo que ya habló con ellos). A learner taught total backshift will mark normal Colombian speech as an error and misjudge what speakers imply.
authority: Backshift in Spanish is not automatic when the content still holds or with a retained preterite: NGLE ch. 24 (tiempos verbales, sequence of tenses), Butt and Benjamin on reported speech. Secondary support: Universidad de Trieste handout on estilo indirecto (Dijo que vendrá hoy a las 5 before 5 pm the next day). NGLE not directly accessed.
replacement: When you retell a conversation after the fact, the verbs usually take one step back, in time and in place, just as in English. Two things can stop that. If what was said still holds right now, you can keep the tense: *Dijo que viene mañana*, if tomorrow has not come yet. And a plain past often stays as it is: *Dijo que ya habló con ellos.*

quote: ¿No solo estudias español, sino también trabajas en español?
problem: Sino before a finite verb needs que. This row targets the structure being taught, so the learner is drilled in the error.
authority: DPD sino: when finite clauses are opposed, sino must be followed by que (via search summary, rae.es/dpd/sino returned 403). FundéuRAE recommends no solo..., sino (también). Usage is looser in speech, but formal Spanish and this lesson's register want que.
replacement: ¿No solo estudias español, sino que también trabajas en español?

quote: ¿Tus vecinos no solo hablan mucho, sino también ayudan?
problem: As u44-t-argument-markers-0028.
authority: DPD sino: when finite clauses are opposed, sino must be followed by que (via search summary, rae.es/dpd/sino returned 403). FundéuRAE recommends no solo..., sino (también). Usage is looser in speech, but formal Spanish and this lesson's register want que.
replacement: ¿Tus vecinos no solo hablan mucho, sino que también ayudan?

quote: English softens with "I was wondering…", "could you possibly…" and "I imagine…". Spanish has four matching moves.
problem: Quisiera, the central Spanish softener, is not in this script. 106 of the 120 bank rows targeting g:softening contain it. Measured: only 3 of 916 scripts mention quisiera, all incidentally, none explains it, and no chunk holds it. It first appears in the bank at u40. An unexplained past subjunctive with no trigger undermines everything the learner was told about the subjunctive.
authority: Measured with a script. NGLE 24.2c, via UDEP, on -ra equivalent to the conditional.
replacement:
English softens with "I was wondering…", "could you possibly…" and "I imagine…". Spanish has five matching moves.

*Quisiera* ("I would like") is the politest opener of all. It looks like the past wish form, but here it stands alone with no *que* in front: *Quisiera saber si hay mesa.*

quote: Aunque llegue tarde, Rosa siempre guardaba una mesa.
problem: Present subjunctive under a past habitual main verb, in a row targeting the structure, with no subject for llegue. The English has someone and arrived, so the two sides do not match either. It is the only such row my scan found in the 14,063 B2 rows.
authority: Sequence of tenses; regex scan of the B2 bank.
replacement: {"es": "Aunque alguien llegara tarde, Rosa siempre guardaba una mesa.", "en": "Even if someone arrived late, Rosa always kept a table."}
